name: Plantar Heel Pain (Plantar Fasciopathy)
summary: The plantar fascia is a strong band of tissue under the foot that runs from the heel bone (calcaneus) to the base of the toes and supports the arch. Plantar heel pain is pain under the heel, most often at the inner (medial) edge of the heel bone where the fascia attaches.

looksLike: Sharp or stabbing pain under the heel with the first steps in the morning or after sitting, which eases after a few minutes of walking and may return later in the day.
Pain with prolonged standing, walking or running, and when walking barefoot or in thin shoes.
Tenderness at the inner edge of the heel bone.
Usually on one side, but it can affect both.
redFlags: Sudden tearing pain with a pop and swelling or bruising
Squeeze test positive or pain with impact in a runner or after a rise in training
Hot, red, swollen heel with fever
Diabetes with an open wound or loss of sensation
Constant night pain, weight loss, swelling or a lump
Bilateral heel pain with morning stiffness, other joints, eye or skin changes
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, load management, strengthening and stretching, supportive footwear.
Justifying findings: first-step pain, medial heel tenderness, positive windlass test, negative squeeze test.
Priority: build load tolerance of the fascia and calf.

assess: Observe foot posture, arch height, swelling, skin and footwear wear.
Palpate the medial calcaneal tubercle, the plantar fascia along the arch, the heel pad, the Achilles insertion and the tarsal tunnel area.
Ankle dorsiflexion range (knee straight and bent) and calf flexibility.
Neurological screen: sensation and Tinel test over the tarsal tunnel.
Strength and single-leg heel raise capacity.
Lumbar and S1 screen if symptoms suggest a nerve root source.

blocks.text: The **plantar fascia** is a strong band of tissue under the foot that runs from the heel bone (calcaneus) to the base of the toes and supports the arch. **Plantar heel pain** is pain under the heel, most often at the inner (medial) edge of the heel bone where the fascia attaches. The most common cause is **plantar fasciopathy** (older name: plantar fasciitis), which is thought to be a load-related problem of the fascia and its attachment rather than a simple inflammation [Ref - to verify].

Risk factors include a recent increase in standing, walking or running, higher body weight, reduced ankle dorsiflexion, a tight calf and hard or thin footwear [Ref - to verify]. Heel spurs on X-ray are common in people without pain and are not the cause of the pain in most cases.
The condition usually improves over months, and most people recover within about a year, although some take longer [Ref - to verify].

items: Sharp or stabbing pain under the heel with the **first steps in the morning** or after sitting, which eases after a few minutes of walking and may return later in the day.
Pain with prolonged standing, walking or running, and when walking barefoot or in thin shoes.
Tenderness at the inner edge of the heel bone.
Usually on one side, but it can affect both.

blocks.text: Honest note: plantar fasciopathy is mainly a clinical diagnosis from the history and the location of the tenderness. The tests below support it and help exclude other causes.
E1. Windlass test

rows: Tighten the plantar fascia by extending the big toe to see whether it reproduces the heel pain
Standing with weight on both feet (weight-bearing version), or sitting with the foot relaxed and the ankle in neutral (non-weight-bearing version)
Kneeling in front of the foot
Passively extend (dorsiflex) the big toe at the joint while the ankle stays still. Hold for up to about 30 seconds and ask about heel pain
Reproduction of the patient's familiar heel pain
No pain or only a stretch sensation at the toe
Plantar fasciopathy, mainly when combined with local tenderness
Reported accuracy varies, and the weight-bearing version may be more sensitive. A negative test does not exclude the condition [Ref - to verify]
Moving the ankle during the test; forcing the toe too far; counting toe-joint pain as positive
If positive, check calf flexibility and begin the fasciopathy plan

blocks.text: E2. Palpation of the medial calcaneal tubercle

rows: Press firmly on the inner side of the underside of the heel bone and along the first part of the fascia
Localised tenderness that reproduces the familiar pain
A tender heel pad or stress fracture may also be tender, so combine with other findings

blocks.text: E3. Calcaneal squeeze test

rows: Squeeze the heel bone from both sides with both hands
Calcaneal stress fracture rather than plantar fasciopathy; refer for imaging

blocks.text: E4. Tarsal tunnel Tinel test and sensation

Tap gently behind and below the inner ankle bone (medial malleolus). **Positive:** tingling or electric sensation into the heel or sole. This suggests nerve entrapment, and a neurological opinion may be needed.
E5. Ankle dorsiflexion and calf flexibility
Use the knee-to-wall test or a goniometer with the knee straight and bent. Reduced dorsiflexion is common with plantar heel pain, although its role as a cause is not proven [Ref - to verify].

Protect; refer if severe or unable to bear weight

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.
Heel pain with first-step morning pain, tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle, a positive windlass test, and a negative squeeze test? **Yes:** working diagnosis is plantar fasciopathy.
Burning or tingling? **Yes:** consider nerve entrapment.
Squeeze positive? **Yes:** consider stress fracture and refer.
If typical, start education, load management and strengthening; add stretching, footwear and an orthosis based on the patient's response.
If no improvement after a suitable trial, review the diagnosis and consider medical options.

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** education and a loading program. Manual therapy is an optional short-term adjunct and does not replace exercise. Do not claim that manual therapy removes a heel spur or breaks down the fascia.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

blocks.text: **Principle:** a plan combining education, loading of the plantar fascia and calf, stretching, and footwear or orthosis support is generally used. High-load strengthening has shown benefit over stretching alone in at least one trial [Ref - to verify]. Effects of different treatments are often modest, and recovery is gradual.

rows: Sit, cross the foot over the knee, pull the toes
back until you feel a stretch in the arch
daily; start before getting out of bed
Lean into a wall with the back leg straight, then bent
High-load heel raise with a rolled towel under the toes
Stand with the toes lifted on a rolled towel, rise onto the toes slowly (about 3 seconds up, 2-second pause, 3 seconds down)
3 sets, starting at about 12 reps and reducing as load increases, 3 days a week [Ref - to verify]
Pain 4 out of 10 or less; add a backpack for load
Pain above 5 out of 10 or lasting into the next day
Draw the ball of the foot toward the heel without curling the toes

blocks.text: **Symptom rule:** pain up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 during exercise that settles within 24 hours is acceptable. First-step pain the next morning should not become much worse.

**Load management:** reduce, rather than stop, painful activities (long standing, hard surfaces, barefoot walking, running distance). Replace some running with cycling or swimming for a time and build running back gradually.
**Footwear and orthoses:**

rows: Avoid thin flat shoes and barefoot walking on hard floors in the early weeks
Short-term pain relief, especially with a high or low arch or a trial to off-load the heel
Benefit is modest and mostly short term [Ref - to verify]
Use to allow activity; effect is temporary [Ref - to verify]
Evidence is limited and comfort varies [Ref - to verify]
Cold (rolling the foot over a frozen bottle)
Option for persistent pain after several months of care
Evidence is mixed and depends on the dose [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: **Medical options (decided by doctors):** corticosteroid injection may give short-term relief but is associated with risks such as fat pad thinning and fascia rupture, so it is used with caution [Ref - to verify]. Other injections and surgery are for persistent cases after a long course of non-surgical care.

blocks.text: **Case:** A 45-year-old nurse has 3 months of sharp pain under the left heel with her first steps in the morning, easing after a few minutes but returning at the end of a shift. She increased her walking recently and wears thin flat shoes. Tenderness is at the inner edge of the heel, the windlass test reproduces her pain, and the squeeze test is negative. Sensation is normal.

**Working diagnosis:** plantar fasciopathy. **Plan:** education, supportive cushioned shoes, plantar fascia and calf stretching, a progressive high-load heel raise program, taping or an orthosis for the start if helpful, and review in 3 to 4 weeks.
**Questions and answers**

items: Why is the heel spur on X-ray not the explanation? Spurs are common in people without pain and many people with plantar heel pain have no spur, so the pain is not explained by the spur itself [Ref - to verify].

Why is first-step pain typical? The fascia shortens and stiffens at rest and gets loaded suddenly on standing, which provokes pain until it warms up. This explanation is accepted but not fully proven.
A runner has pain with impact and a positive squeeze test. What now? Suspect a calcaneal stress fracture, stop loading and refer for imaging.
Why use heel raises rather than only stretching? A trial found that high-load strengthening gave better outcomes than stretching alone [Ref - to verify].
Why is repeated steroid injection discouraged? There is a risk of fat pad thinning and fascia rupture and long-term benefit is limited [Ref - to verify].
**Initial approach:** education, load management, strengthening and stretching, supportive footwear.
**Justifying findings:** first-step pain, medial heel tenderness, positive windlass test, negative squeeze test.
**Priority:** build load tolerance of the fascia and calf.
**Manual therapy:** minor adjunct.
**Exercise:** plantar fascia stretch, calf stretch, high-load heel raises, foot intrinsic work.
**Modalities:** limited role; shockwave for persistent cases.
**Tell the patient:** common, usually improves over months, and not caused by a spur.
**Avoid:** barefoot walking on hard floors early, repeated steroid injections, ignoring squeeze pain.
**Measure:** first-step pain, task pain, dorsiflexion, heel raise capacity, questionnaire.
**If no improvement:** review diagnosis and consider specialist options.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** pain controlled and function restored with a maintenance plan.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** adult, no stress fracture, no nerve entrapment, no systemic disease.

items: **Can be tested:** whether strengthening, stretching, orthoses, taping and shockwave improve pain; how to predict who recovers slowly.
**Hypotheses:** that tissue load capacity, not inflammation, drives symptoms.
**Future questions:** best exercise dose, and the role of weight loss and footwear changes.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.

sections.A: Plantar fascia pair ke neeche edi se ungliyon tak mazboot patti hai. Jab is par load bardasht se zyada ho to edi ke neeche dard hota hai.
sections.B: Subah ke pehle qadmon ya baithne ke baad edi ke neeche tez chubhta dard, jo thora chalne se kam aur zyada khade rehne se phir barhta hai.
sections.C: Kya dard aaraam ke baad pehle qadmon par sab se zyada hai, dard kahan hai, aur kya kaam ya joote badle.
sections.D: Pair ki shakal, arch, sujan, joote, chaal aur edi ke andar ki taraf dabana.
sections.E: Yeh zyada tar clinical diagnosis hai: history aur dard ki jagah. Windlass test madadgar hai. Heel spur dard ki wajah sabit nahi karta.
sections.F: Heel fat pad, calcaneal stress fracture aur nerve ka dabna isi jaise lag sakte hain.
sections.G: Achanak pop ke saath dard aur sujan (fascia phatna), ya squeeze test positive (stress fracture): refer.
sections.H: Red flags na hon, subah ke pehle qadmon ka dard aur edi ke andar dabane par dard: plantar fasciopathy.
sections.I: Pindli aur fascia par soft tissue kaam, aur takhne ki mobilisation.
sections.J: Education, fascia aur pindli ka loading (jaise heel raises), stretching aur zaroorat ho to taping ya insoles.
sections.K: Barf (thandi bottle par pair ghumana) aur TENS optional; lambe dard mein shockwave.
sections.L: Diagnosis confirm karein, samjhayein ke yeh mahinon mein theek hota hai, load control aur exercise shuru.
sections.M: Pehle qadmon ka dard, 10 minute chalne ka dard, windlass aur taaqat dobara dekhein.
sections.N: 45 saal ki nurse ko 3 mahine se subah edi ke neeche dard hai. Khud socho, phir jawab dekho.
